title: Multi-criteria routing synthesis and decision-tree notes
content:
Purpose
---
Notes and working synthesis for a multi-criteria routing policy that balances latency, cost, and reliability across hosted/dedicated/private deployments and multiple regions. This doc is intentionally tactical: concrete thresholds, a compact decision tree, config knobs, and control-plane interactions.

Background / goals
- Users expect predictable tail latency for interactive inference (SLOs), but cost constraints and capacity limits force tradeoffs.
- Routing policy should be expressible as a small set of weighted signals plus hard gates for safety.
- Must be implementable in the control plane without heavy per-request compute; decisions can be cached and reevaluated when telemetry changes.

Design principles
- Keep primary decision path O(1) per request: precompute score tables for (route, model_variant, region) tuples with a short-circuit for hard failures.
- Separate 'policy language' (declarative weights/thresholds) from runtime heuristics (smoothing, decay, cooldowns).
- Prefer observable, debuggable heuristics over opaque ML-based scorers in the first iteration.

Signals we use
- p50/p95/p99 latency (observed) for route/model/region aggregation
- per-route cost_per_token estimate (derived from throughput and instance type)
- availability: fraction of successful requests over window (error-rate, OOMs, timeouts)
- capacity headroom: queued requests vs concurrency limits per pool
- model-quality tag: whether the variant is flagged for quality regression or drift
- routing-tier: customer tier (free, standard, enterprise)
- region preference: data locality constraints or customer pinning

Policy structure (conceptual)
1) Hard gates (fail-open/closed):
  - If availability < 90% for a given route+variant => exclude unless no alternatives.
  - If model-quality == degraded => exclude for enterprise customers; warn for standard.
  - If region is pinned by policy => only consider pinned region(s).
2) Scoring function: score = -w_lat * norm_latency + w_cost * norm_cost_savings + w_rel * norm_reliability + w_pref * client_pref
  - norm_* are normalized scalars in [0,1] updated every evaluation window (5m default).
  - We treat latency as negative (lower is better). Cost_savings positive if cheaper than baseline.
3) Decision: pick highest-scoring candidate; apply soft-fallbacks (stepdown to slightly lower quality but much cheaper variant) if score delta > fallback_threshold.

Concrete config example (numbers are draft)
- eval_window: 5m
- p95_thresholds: fast=150ms, medium=350ms, slow=750ms
- costs normalized against baseline xLargeGPU: baseline=1.0, quantized variant=0.45, distill-small=0.20
- weights: w_lat=0.6, w_cost=0.25, w_rel=0.1, w_pref=0.05
- availability_gate=0.90
- fallback_score_gap=0.15

Why these numbers?
- Latency dominates user-perceived quality for chat/interactive flows; we put most weight on latency.
- Cost matters for heavy throughput customers and background batch workloads; keep non-zero weight so control plane sometimes chooses cheaper variants for non-critical routes.

Decision-tree (ascii, simplified)

INCOMING_REQUEST -> apply_hard_gates -> gather_candidates -> score_candidates -> if score_gap_to_next > fallback_score_gap then select primary else select highest score -> apply_rate_limits_and_throttles -> route_request

Expanded decision tree (text)
1) apply_hard_gates:
   - if region pinned: candidates = variants_in_region; else candidates = all_variants
   - remove candidates where availability < availability_gate (unless candidates become empty)
   - remove candidates with model_quality == degraded for high-tier customers
2) gather_candidates: attach telemetry (p95, cost, headroom) and client metadata (tier, latency_sensitivity flag)
3) score_candidates: normalize signals by precomputed moving windows; compute weighted sum
4) select & fallback: if top candidate has a high score and enough capacity, route. If top candidate is slightly better but nearing capacity, consider next candidate if cost saving is large or latency impact acceptable

Short pseudocode (procedural)
- Input: request_metadata, route_config
- candidates = config.variants
- candidates = filter_hard_gates(candidates, request_metadata)
- if candidates empty: escalate -> use global-fallback-route (lower tier) with circuit-breaker flag
- for c in candidates: c.score = score(c.telemetry, request_metadata)
- sort candidates by score desc
- top = candidates[0]; second = candidates[1] if len>1 else null
- if second and (top.score - second.score) < fallback_score_gap and top.headroom < headroom_threshold: choose second
- else choose top

Control plane implementation notes
- Telemetry update cadence: aggregated windows every 1m and rolling 5m; control plane caches scores for 10s to reduce churn.
- Use a central policy evaluator service that writes precomputed route tables to regional edge caches; edge makes O(1) lookup for requests.
- Safety: every policy change must go through an audit trail and staged rollout (console -> canary -> global).

Multi-region considerations
- Prefer local region if latency delta < 20ms and availability >= availability_gate.
- Cross-region routing only if local capacity is constrained or local availability degraded. Add explicit cost penalty for cross-region egress to bias toward local.
- Respect data residency: if customer has region_pin, obey it (hard gate).

Tiered behavior examples
- Free tier: stronger cost weight (w_cost up), allow noisier fallbacks, but stricter rate limiting.
- Enterprise: stricter availability and quality gates, allow cross-region fallback only to enterprise-dedicated pools with SLA.

Edge cases and failure modes
- Synchronized spikes: many edges see capacity drop and try to failover to same candidate -> overload. Mitigation: probabilistic spillover + global capacity governor.
- Flapping: telemetry oscillates causing frequent routing flips. Mitigation: hysteresis (cooldown 30s), require sustained delta over two windows.
- Black-swan region outage: have a global emergency path that rejects low-priority work and routes only enterprise-critical traffic.

Observability and debugging
- Expose per-request routing decision metadata header (route-id, score breakdown, reasoning_code). Keep header short but sufficient for debugging.
- Console views: per-route distribution of chosen variants, fallback rates, score histograms, and map of region-to-region fallbacks.
- Alerting: when fallback_rate > 5% for > 10m or when headroom < 10% for two or more regions for same pool.

Open questions and follow-ups
- Do we want an ML-based reranker in the control plane later? If so, start with a small offline model that predicts user-perceived latency-quality tradeoff.
- Should we make weight tuning per-route automatic (optimize for cost under latency SLO)? Experiment: simulated annealing on historical traces.
- How to represent model-quality signals from evaluations more systematically (link eval jobs to routing flags).

Next actions (short-term)
- Implement scoring library + policy format in GH:infra/routing-config (owner: Maya)
- Small canary: add header debugging metadata for 5 routes and watch fallback rates (owner: Ava)
- Run retrospective on two recent incidents and replay routing decisions against traces to validate heuristics (owner: Diego)

Appendix: example score breakdown (sample top candidate)
- normalized_latency = 0.85 (p95 120ms \u2192 good)
- normalized_cost_savings = 0.35 (quantized variant)
- normalized_reliability = 0.98
- client_pref = 0.0
score = -0.6*0.85 + 0.25*0.35 + 0.1*0.98 + 0.05*0.0 = -0.51 + 0.0875 + 0.098 = -0.3245 -> higher is better (note sign convention: we invert latency when normalizing in implementation)

Notes to reviewers
- This is a working doc; please annotate with examples from your workload and propose adjustments to weights. I deliberately kept the initial scoring simple so we can iterate.
